analysis.one_liner: Makes failed-bank executives return up to five years of pay when their bank collapses.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on the bill; it was referred to the Financial Services Committee in April 2023, won 4 bipartisan cosponsors, and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a bank fails and the FDIC takes it over, the FDIC spends insured depositors' money and its own rescue costs to make depositors whole. This bill would let the FDIC take back up to five years of salary, bonuses, stock awards, and stock-trading profits from any executive substantially responsible for the failure, and would make the bank's parent holding company cover the FDIC's costs before any other creditors or shareholders get paid. The money would go into the Deposit Insurance Fund or the Treasury.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers and the deposit insurance system. The FDIC's rescue fund — which ordinary depositors ultimately stand behind — would be repaid by the executives who ran a failed bank and by its holding company, instead of losses falling on the fund, on other banks, or on unsecured depositors.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and the deposit insurance fund

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FDIC to claw back all or part of five years of compensation — salary, bonuses, performance- and equity-based awards, and profits from buying or selling securities — from any institution-affiliated party substantially responsible for a failed bank's condition, so that party bears losses consistent with their responsibility [S2][S3].
Applies the same clawback to the largest financial companies in Dodd-Frank orderly liquidation, not just small insured banks [S3].

Makes a failed bank's holding company liable to the FDIC for payments to insured depositors, the FDIC's receivership costs, and interest, secured by a first-priority lien on all holding-company assets, with no payment to any other creditor or shareholder until the FDIC is paid in full [S2][S3].
Sends recovered compensation into the Deposit Insurance Fund or the general fund of the Treasury rather than to private parties [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Executives who were substantially responsible for a bank's failure — they would return compensation received over the previous five years — plus bank holding companies and their shareholders, who would absorb the FDIC's rescue costs ahead of any other distribution.
analysis.who_pays_short: Executives of failed banks and holding companies

drawbacks.text: The clawback turns on who is 'substantially responsible' for a failure, a judgment that would invite years of litigation and disputes over how much of each executive's pay to recover [S3].

A standing five-year pay clawback gives bank executives a new reason to negotiate larger guaranteed salaries, shift compensation abroad or into hard-to-recover forms, and could make it harder for troubled banks to recruit the leadership needed to fix themselves.

Giving the FDIC's holding-company claim automatic priority over all other liens and over bankruptcy proceedings changes long-settled creditor rules, which other creditors of bank holding companies would contest [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is narrow and well-targeted: it applies only after a bank actually fails and only to people substantially responsible, so the cost falls on a small group that did the damage rather than on the industry generally or on consumers. The main real costs are litigation over responsibility and possible effects on executive recruitment at weak banks. On balance the safeguards for the deposit insurance fund outweigh those costs, though the bill does not address the supervisory failures that let banks fail in the first place.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2023 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up, and the session ended without a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Katie Porter introduced the Failed Bank Executives Clawback Act on April 27, 2023, to amend the Federal Deposit Insurance Act so the FDIC can claw back compensation from executives substantially responsible for a bank failure [S1][S3].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services; the action history shows no further action — no markup, no floor vote — for the remainder of the 118th Congress [S5].
It drew four cosponsors, two Democrats and two Republicans: Reps. Victoria Spartz (R-IN), Ken Buck (R-CO), Ruben Gallego (D-AZ), and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-WA) [S4].

The bill came amid the 2023 regional bank failures, in which the FDIC resolved Silicon Valley Bank, Signature Bank, and First Republic and bore large costs protecting uninsured depositors; the bill would have shifted some of those costs to the executives and holding companies behind such failures.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executives of failed banks and their holding companies kept their compensation and faced no FDIC clawback; the deposit insurance fund and taxpayers continue to absorb resolution costs.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Democrat with a split-bill slate of two Republican and two Democratic cosponsors; no chamber vote ever occurred, so no roll-call breakdown exists.

industries.industry: Executives of failed banks and large financial companies
industries.note: Would have to return up to five years of salary, bonuses, equity awards, and securities-trading profits if substantially responsible for a bank's failure. Their gain in the current system is that resolution costs fall on the FDIC fund instead.
Would become liable to the FDIC for depositor payouts and receivership costs, with a first-priority lien on all assets and payment behind no one until the FDIC is made whole.

Well-run banks would face no direct clawback, but the industry funds the Deposit Insurance Fund that absorbs failure costs today; the bill would shift those costs to failed institutions' own executives and holding companies.
